\paragraph{Practical implications.}\looseness=-1
The three-way decomposition---inherited gating, training-associated integration, and exit collapse---carries direct consequences for VLA development.
Mid-layer features (peak at L9--L11) consistently outperform exit-layer representations for action prediction where collapse is pronounced (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_practical_implications}), suggesting that practitioners building downstream modules (e.g., skill selectors, safety monitors) should tap mid-layer rather than final-layer representations.
The distinction between VLM-to-VLA and VLA-to-VLA transitions matters for continual learning: VLA-to-VLA fine-tuning preserves exit-layer structure ($\Delta R^2 < 0.10$), while VLM-to-VLA training disrupts it---implying that warm-starting from a general-purpose VLA may be more representation-preserving than fine-tuning a VLM directly.
The inherited nature of L1 attention further suggests that backbone selection shapes instruction routing before any robot data is seen; this prior structure may constrain or enable downstream instruction following.

\paragraph{Limitations.}\looseness=-1
Our conclusions rest on $N{=}2$ VLM-to-VLA transitions plus one VLA-to-VLA case, all causal decoders on a single benchmark (LIBERO); flow-matching~\cite{black2024_pi0} and diffusion~\cite{ghosh2024_octo} heads may differ.

Closed-loop validation and intermediate-checkpoint dynamics~\cite{grant2026,haon2025} are priorities.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}\looseness=-1
We decompose VLA instruction routing into entry gating, mid-layer integration, and exit collapse---consistent across three architectures, two training pathways, and four instruction conditions. $\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ offers a probe-based screening signal supplementing rollout evaluation.
